heuristics.rule: Every job switch should deliver at least one of: higher salary, promotion, brand-name project experience, or alignment with genuine interest
heuristics.condition: When considering whether to switch jobs
heuristics.action: Audit the opportunity against these four dimensions before committing; if none apply, reconsider
heuristics.because: Commenter explicitly states that each switch must achieve one of these or it is aimless movement, not career progression

heuristics.rule: Benchmark yourself on the job market continuously, not only when you decide to switch
heuristics.condition: When assessing your own market value at any career stage
heuristics.action: Regularly review job postings for peer roles to calibrate your actual skill level and compensation
heuristics.because: Commenter argues self-evaluation is systematically inflated; external market comparison is the corrective, and HR uses the same comparison to evaluate candidates

heuristics.rule: Treat job requirements as a skill progression map ('experience bar') to gamify and direct your development
heuristics.condition: When you feel unclear about what to work on next in your career
heuristics.action: Map concrete job posting requirements to specific deliverables and assign yourself milestone targets
heuristics.because: Commenter describes this framework explicitly as a way to make career progress visible and motivation-sustaining, analogous to game progress bars

heuristics.rule: Clarify the new team's expectations in the first weeks of joining, not after problems arise
heuristics.condition: When onboarding at a new company
heuristics.action: Proactively ask your manager and peers what success looks like at every level — from weekly deliverables to your long-term role
heuristics.because: Best-answer author describes leaving a promising role after half a month specifically because he failed to surface team product expectations early enough; mature teams have low tolerance for new hire misalignment

heuristics.rule: If an interviewer focuses only on technical skills and shows no curiosity about who you are as a person, treat it as a signal to decline
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a potential employer during the interview process
heuristics.action: Assess whether the interview is genuinely two-directional; one-sided skill interrogation indicates a team culture problem
heuristics.because: Best-answer author states this explicitly as a filtering heuristic — team quality is revealed by how they conduct hiring

decision_factors.factor: Team culture revealed during interview process
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A team that treats interviews as purely technical screenings likely doesn't invest in people; this predicts your experience post-join
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask substantive questions about product vision and team composition; observe whether the interviewer engages with you as a person or only tests skills

decision_factors.factor: Whether the new role offers love for the product and a sense of mission
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The best-answer author (a PM) argues that without these two emotional connections, the work will be unsustainable regardless of compensation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask yourself: do I use this product daily? Do I believe in what this team is building? If neither, flag it

decision_factors.factor: Social insurance (social security / health insurance) continuity
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Gaps in social insurance affect housing purchase eligibility, medical access, residency permits, and household registration in Chinese cities
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate the gap between last day at current employer and first day at new employer; if over 15 days, arrange self-payment to avoid lapse

decision_factors.factor: Primary goal for the next role (experience, skills, salary, network, growth)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Without a clear priority, you cannot evaluate competing offers rationally and will default to salary as a tiebreaker even if it isn't what you need most
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Write down your single most important goal before looking at opportunities; use it as the primary filter

decision_factors.factor: Team orientation (KPI-driven vs. outcome-driven vs. learning-driven)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Team orientation directly determines your day-to-day work experience and what you will learn; misalignment causes rapid disengagement
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the hiring manager explicitly: 'What does success look like for this team in 6 months?' and 'How do you measure individual contribution?'

decision_factors.factor: Financial buffer to avoid rushed decisions
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Without at least 2 months of savings, economic pressure forces acceptance of suboptimal offers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate your monthly fixed expenses; confirm you have at least 2 months covered before resigning without another offer in hand

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Switching jobs while employed (moonlighting your job search)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You cannot fully commit to either the old job or the new search; the best-answer author argues this creates dissatisfaction in both directions and disrespects both parties
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who try to reduce risk by job-hunting while still employed without telling their current employer

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a startup or small team without clarifying expectations upfront
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Mature startup teams have very low error tolerance for new hires; misaligned expectations in the first month can result in departure before you've had a chance to contribute
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Experienced PMs joining smaller teams who assume their seniority will give them time to figure out the role

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Optimizing for salary as the primary switching criterion
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Salary-chasing without industry trajectory analysis can lock you into a declining sector; short-term gains are erased by long-term obsolescence
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals who are competent but not yet senior enough to see industry-level trends

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Resigning without documenting and transferring admin/system access
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Oversight creates loose ends that damage your professional reputation; in internet roles with many platform integrations, this is easy to miss
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs and operators who accumulated access across many tools and projects over multi-year tenures

failure_patterns.pattern: Emotional or reactive resignation — quitting after a conflict without strategic planning
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: In-the-moment frustration overrides long-term reasoning; the pain of staying feels greater than the uncertainty of leaving
failure_patterns.consequence: The underlying interpersonal or execution problem follows you to the next role; the commenter states 'if you couldn't make it work here, you won't there either'
warning_signs: The decision to leave followed a specific argument or incident rather than a pattern
You haven't identified what you're moving toward, only what you're fleeing

failure_patterns.pattern: Herd-following job switches during 'golden hiring season'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Social contagion — seeing colleagues interview creates FOMO and normalizes switching even without personal readiness
failure_patterns.consequence: Switches made without self-assessment land in roles that don't advance your career; you arrive at a new company without clear goals
warning_signs: You started thinking about switching after a colleague announced their departure
You cannot articulate what specifically you want from the new role

failure_patterns.pattern: Overestimating personal market value when detached from a well-known company
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Attribution error — confusing company brand for personal capability; the 'halo effect' of a large employer inflates perceived individual worth
failure_patterns.consequence: Shock when the market doesn't respond to your candidacy as expected; offers come in lower than anticipated
warning_signs: Your confidence in switching is primarily based on your current company's reputation
You haven't independently validated your skills against job postings in the last year

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to surface team expectations in the first weeks of a new role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: New hires feel pressure to demonstrate competence by doing, not asking; onboarding urgency suppresses curiosity about alignment
failure_patterns.consequence: Best-answer author left a promising opportunity after half a month because misalignment was discovered too late; in mature teams there is little recovery room
warning_signs: You have not explicitly discussed what your manager expects you to deliver in the first 30/60/90 days
You are defaulting to your previous company's ways of working without validating fit

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you name the single most important thing you want to gain from this next role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the switch is goal-directed or reactive; vague answers indicate the person is running away rather than running toward
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Does the specific opportunity you're considering actually deliver that thing — or are you rationalizing?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You are not ready to switch yet; take two weeks to clarify your priority before engaging with any opportunity

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you use the product you would be working on daily, and do you feel a sense of mission about it?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: For PMs specifically, absence of both signals the role will feel hollow regardless of compensation or title
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are those feelings durable — would they survive learning the messy internal reality of the company?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The best-answer author treats this as a hard filter: if neither condition is foreseeable, it is not the right move

diagnostic_questions.question: When you compare your current skill profile to job postings for your target next level, what specific gaps appear?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has done an honest market calibration or is relying on internal self-assessment alone
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are those gaps closeable in your current role, or do you need external experience to close them?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The person has not yet done this exercise; recommend doing it before deciding to switch

diagnostic_questions.question: Did the interviewer ask about who you are as a person, or only about your technical skills?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the hiring team is investing in cultural and interpersonal fit, which predicts team health
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What specific questions did they ask — were they genuine or formulaic?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a warning signal about team culture; treat it as a reason to probe further or decline

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have at least two months of living expenses saved?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether economic pressure will force a rushed decision, degrading offer quality
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Then you have negotiating leverage; don't accept the first offer out of fear
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Prioritize building this buffer before resigning, or secure the next offer before leaving

industry_realities.common_belief: Your value in the market is roughly equivalent to your performance at your current company
industry_realities.actual_reality: Much of what feels like personal achievement is attributable to the company brand, team infrastructure, and resources; stripped of that context, market response is often significantly lower
industry_realities.implication: Do a real market test — apply and interview — before anchoring your self-assessment to internal performance reviews or titles

industry_realities.common_belief: The 'golden hiring season' (March-April post-Lunar New Year) is the best time to switch
industry_realities.actual_reality: The season creates more competition, herd behavior, and rushed decisions; the best time to switch is when you are genuinely ready, not when the calendar suggests it
industry_realities.implication: Seasonal timing should be a secondary factor, not a trigger; avoid switching just because others are

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary data from published reports accurately reflects the market
industry_realities.actual_reality: A commenter explicitly notes that published salary reports (e.g. Lagou 2014 data cited) skew approximately 25% high; they are directionally useful but not reliable for precise negotiation
industry_realities.implication: Use salary benchmarks as rough orientation, not as justification for a specific ask; triangulate with multiple sources

industry_realities.common_belief: Internet industry salaries rise indefinitely and the sector is always growing
industry_realities.actual_reality: The post (written in a period of optimism) assumes continuous growth, but the industry reality is that sectors mature, consolidate, and shed workers; choosing an industry without assessing its trajectory is a long-term risk
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate the 10-year arc of the sector you're entering, not just current compensation data

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Evaluates self against internal peers and manager feedback; feels confident about market value without testing it externally
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Continuously benchmarks against job postings; treats internal feedback as one data point and market response as the ground truth
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overconfidence from internal metrics leads to poor negotiating positions and surprise at offer levels

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Reacts to a negative event (conflict, low bonus, peer's departure) and justifies the switch post-hoc
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Has a clear answer to 'what do I need to gain from this next role?' before evaluating any opportunity
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Reactive switches optimize for escape, not progression; they often recreate the same problems in a new environment

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Onboarding behavior at a new company
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Dives into doing the work assuming goals are understood; waits until a problem surfaces to clarify expectations
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Proactively elicits explicit expectations from manager and peers in week one — from immediate deliverables to long-term role definition
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Mature teams have low tolerance for misalignment; discovering it after the fact is often unrecoverable in the first month

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Reads job postings only when actively job searching; uses them as checklists to pass interviews
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Uses job postings as a continuous development map — identifying skill gaps and setting deliberate learning goals between switches
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Reactive skill-building creates lag; proactive development means you're already qualified before you start searching

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Views career as a series of company decisions; switches companies to solve problems
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Views career as personal brand management; each role, departure, and transition either builds or damages a long-term professional reputation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: In tight industry networks (especially internet/tech), how you leave is as visible as where you go next

community_misconceptions.misconception: Frequent job-hopping shows ambition and increases your market value
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Each switch often comes with a salary bump, creating the illusion that more switches equal more growth
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Frequent switching prevents skill accumulation, signals low loyalty, and makes HR and hiring managers question whether you'll leave them too; it reduces your chances of being placed in high-trust or senior roles
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: You are consistently considered for execution roles but not leadership or strategic positions; the resume pattern becomes a ceiling

community_misconceptions.misconception: If you're unhappy, switching companies will fix the problem
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The new environment feels different initially, providing temporary relief that confirms the theory
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Interpersonal, communication, and execution problems are personal patterns that follow you; if the root cause is your behavior or mindset, it reappears in the new role
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Serial unhappiness across companies with no self-insight into the common variable — yourself

community_misconceptions.misconception: Verbal promises about salary, benefits, and scope made during the interview are binding
community_misconceptions.why_believed: People in excited negotiation states want to believe commitments are genuine; challenging them feels aggressive
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Only written, signed offer terms are enforceable; verbal promises are routinely not honored, especially on variable comp, bonus structure, and title
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Arriving at a new job to find take-home pay or benefits differ from what was discussed; no recourse after joining

real_case_outcomes.situation: Senior PM, 4 years at same company, left without a next role secured (bare resignation)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Took approximately 2 weeks off to decompress, reflect, and clarify what he wanted before beginning an active search; returned to a previous employer (now rebranded) with mostly the same team
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Successful re-integration; reflects positively on the decision 4+ years later; sees the return as rational given personal clarity and team quality
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A deliberate buffer period between jobs — used for reflection, not just rest — improves the quality of the next decision; returning to a previous employer is not failure if the team and mission are genuinely aligned

real_case_outcomes.situation: PM joined what he described as a strong team for a half-month trial period
real_case_outcomes.decision: Left after the month because he had not clarified the team's product expectations during the interview or onboarding period
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Departure from a potentially good opportunity; frames it as an own goal caused by assumption rather than due diligence
real_case_outcomes.lesson: In startup or product-driven teams, failing to surface and align on product expectations in the first weeks is a firing offense regardless of competence; this is especially true when the team is small and each role is critical

psychological_barriers.trigger: Considering switching because colleagues are switching or it's hiring season
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Social contagion and FOMO — the behavior of peers normalizes a major decision and reduces the threshold for acting on vague dissatisfaction
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Person asks 'should I also switch?' without articulating what they want; the question is about permission, not strategy
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Redirect immediately: 'What specifically do you want to get from a switch that you cannot get where you are?' If they can't answer, they're not ready

psychological_barriers.trigger: Expressing confidence about market value based on current company's reputation or internal seniority
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Attribution error — conflating company brand with personal capability; the halo effect of a large employer inflates self-assessment
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Statements like 'I've been doing X at Company Y for N years, I should be worth Z in the market' without external validation
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask them to apply to three comparable roles externally and see what happens; actual market feedback is the only antidote to inflated self-assessment

psychological_barriers.trigger: Feeling unable to search for new roles while still employed without feeling guilty or disloyal
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Identity enmeshment with current employer; leaving feels like betrayal rather than a normal career event
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Person delays job search, stays in a suboptimal role too long, or feels they must quit first before looking
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'You are managing your personal brand, not being disloyal. Your employer is simultaneously managing their talent pipeline. Both are normal.'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Feeling rushed to accept an offer because savings are low or current situation is intolerable
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Scarcity mindset — economic pressure narrows cognitive bandwidth and inflates the apparent value of the first available escape
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Accepting offers without negotiating, joining roles that don't meet stated criteria, and regretting it within months
psychological_barriers.expert_move: The financial buffer prescription (2 months savings minimum) is the structural fix; without it, advise building the buffer before resigning rather than trying to decide well under pressure

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I switch jobs? Is now a good time?
reframing_moves.reframe: What do you need to get from your next role — and does your current role have any path to delivering that?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the question from a binary yes/no timing decision to a goal-clarity exercise; forces the person to articulate what they're optimizing for before evaluating any external option
reframing_moves.example_language: 明确想要在下一份工作得到什么 (Clarify what you want to gain from your next job) — the goal must be explicit before any opportunity can be evaluated

reframing_moves.original_framing: I think I'm worth more than my current salary — I should switch for a raise
reframing_moves.reframe: Go look at job postings for your target role right now. What do they require that you don't have yet?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Replaces inflated self-assessment with external market calibration; the gap revealed is more useful than either the confidence or the anxiety
reframing_moves.example_language: 不怕不识货，就怕货比货 (Don't be afraid of not knowing your worth — be afraid of not comparing yourself to the market)

reframing_moves.original_framing: How do I make sure I'm making progress in my career?
reframing_moves.reframe: Treat job requirements as a skill progression map — assign yourself concrete milestones from real postings and track completion like a game
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Converts abstract career anxiety into specific, actionable, measurable tasks; the game metaphor reduces emotional weight and increases motivation
reframing_moves.example_language: 经验条化 (experience-bar-ification) — make your career progress as visible and trackable as a game level bar

reframing_moves.original_framing: My career is about choosing the right companies to work for
reframing_moves.reframe: Your career is about managing your personal brand — every departure, every transition, and every role is a visible data point in a transparent industry
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Expands the time horizon and the audience; shifts from transactional ('get a job') to reputational ('build a track record') thinking
reframing_moves.example_language: 互联网的最大特性就是'透明'，你是好的臭不了，你真搞臭了也遮不住 (The internet's defining feature is transparency — you can't hide quality, and you can't hide damage)
